To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex (MTB complex) is an ancient pathogen that has been infecting animals and humans for thousands of years.

we have identified four clades of animal adapted Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex strains that might correspond to independent host shifts and that host range seems to be driven more by contact rates and population size of the host species than by host relatedness.

the animal adapted members of the Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex are paraphyletic, with one of the ecotypes more closely related to human adapted Mycobaterium africanum than to the other animal adapted ecotypes; the animal adapted ecotypes are associated to specific hosts; the phylogeny of animal adapted MTB strains does not reflect the phylogeny and phylogenetic distance of the host species; and the animal adapted MTB ecotypes might be generalists that adapted to specific hosts
In summary, our research is concerned with
the phylogenetic relationships among the animal adapted Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex (MTB complex).
the phylogenetic relationships between different ecotypes of MTBC and how they have evolved.
the evolution of a bacterial species that causes a devastating disease in humans, but also affects other species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MTBC is not monophyletic, but that it is a polyphyletic group of species, and that there are at most 9 species of the MTBC, and not more.

the animal adapted ecotypes of the Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex (MTC), the cause of tuberculosis (TB) in animals, are not monophyletic and that they evolved independently from the human adapted MTC.
the phylogenetic relationships of the different ecotype members of the MTB complex are not well known and are still under debate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the MTBC is a complex of species that have evolved in a variety of different host species, and the host range of each species is determined not just by the ability to infect a host but also by the ability to persist in the host population.
we have shown that the animal adapted Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex strains are not a monophyletic group and that there is evidence for multiple independent host shifts from humans to animals.
there are four main clades of animal adapted Mycobacterum tuberculosis, and that the host shift to humans occurred from one of the animal adapted clades.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the animal adapted ecotypes are not monophyletic and are not necessarily more closely related to their respective hosts.
there are at most four ecotypes infecting animals other that humans, and that these ecotypes are not monophyletic.
the animal adapted ecotypes of the Mycobacterum tuberculosis complex (MTB complex) are not monophyletic.
